rows.prompt: What memory interface does the i.MX 93 support for external DRAM?
rows.rubric: Answer this knowledge-base question: 'What memory interface does the i.MX 93 support for external DRAM?'. Reference facts (may be incomplete or stale — verify against the SOURCE CONTEXT): ['16-bit', 'LPDDR4']. CORRECT = accurate answer, every claim grounded; ABSTAINED = says the sources don't cover it, or a partial-but-accurate answer; WRONG = fabricated or contradicted facts.
rows.raw:
The i.MX 93 supports external DRAM via a 16-bit wide memory interface. It is capable of supporting LPDDR4X and can have a maximum supported capacity of 2GByte. The memory interface supports the following modes:

- SDR Mode up to 166MHz
- DDR Mode up to 166MHz (with external Flash device DQS input)
- SDR Mode up to 133MHz and DDR Mode up to 66MHz (with internal DQS loopback through DQS pad mode)

For more detailed specifications and configuration, you may want to refer to the i.MX 93 Applications Processor Reference Manual.

This core uses DynamIQ technology, the successor to Arm‘s big.LITTLE concept, and features the latest extensions to the Armv8-A architecture, including a dedicated instruction set for implementing energy-ef- ficient control systems. The „EdgeLock Secure Enclave“ provides further support for the simple implementation of security concepts. The 16-bit memory interface uses LPDDR4 and offers optional internal ECC support. In addition to offering up to four I²S audio interfaces and eight PDM microphone inputs, the processor provides numerous other interfaces. These include CAN-FD, UARTs, SPI, QSPI, I²C, and SDIO. It also has extensive security functions. There are two CPU variants available, which differ mainly in clock frequency. NXP offers the i.MX 91 Processor, an optimized CPU in terms of price and functionality from the i.MX 9 family. The i.MX 91 is the smallest CPU in the i.MX 9 family, alongside the i.MX 93, and it is an excellent alternative to the i.MX 28 and i.MX 6UL/i.MX 6ULL for new designs. Like the rest of the i.MX 9 family, the i.MX 91 is based on the same core architecture. Its main differences are its integrated safety functions, The i.MX 91‘s main interfaces are: • 1x 24-Bit RGB display • 1x 8 Bit RGB camera interface • 3x SDIO/eMMC • 2x USB 2.0 • 2x Gigabit Ethernet (1 x with TSN) • 2x CAN FD • 8x UART, 8x I²C, 8x SPI, 4x I²S • 1x QSPI • 2x FlexIO • 1x Medium quality sound output (Sigma-Delta modulator) network interfaces, and CAN interfaces, including dual Gigabit Ethernet and dual CAN FD. A parallel camera inter- face (8-bit RGB) enables direct connection of a camera to the CPU and supports applications involving basic image processing. This provides a high degree of flexibility in designing a main- board to optimize CPU utilization and ensure maximum efficiency. TQ-Embedded has developed two modules that allow all i.MX 91 and i.MX 93 derivatives to be used in the same design despite CPU differences.

ENET_QOS Ethernet QoS Controller The ENET_QOS is compliant with the IEEE 802.3–2015 specification and can be used in applications, such as AV bridges, AV nodes, switches, data center bridges and nodes, and network interface cards. It enables a host to transmit and receive data over Ethernet in compliance with the IEEE 802.3–2015. The Ethernet QoS with TSN also supports following features: • 802.1Qbv Enhancements to Scheduling Traffic • 802.1Qbu Frame preemption • Time Based Scheduling FlexIO1 FlexIO2 Flexible Input/Output FlexIO is capable of supporting a wide range of protocols, including but not limited to UART, I2C, SPI, I2S, camera interface, display interface, PWM waveform generation, etc. The module can remain functional when the chip is in a low power mode provided the clock it is using remain active. FlexSPI1 Flexible Serial Peripheral Interface The FlexSPI module acts as an interface to one external Octal serial flash devices, or up to two external Quad SPI serial flash devices by two chip select signals, but sharing same CLK/DQS/DATA signals. The i.MX 93 supports an external DRAM (Dynamic Random Access Memory) through a 16-bit wide memory interface. Specifically, it supports LPDDR4X memory technology and can have a maximum supported capacity of 2GByte. For more detailed memory configuration and compatibility, you can refer to the i.MX 93 Applications Processor Reference Manual.

rows.rubric: Answer this knowledge-base question: 'Which peripheral on the i.MX 93 handles UART, and what IP block routes its pins?'. Reference facts (may be incomplete or stale — verify against the SOURCE CONTEXT): ['LPUART', 'IOMUX']. CORRECT = accurate answer, every claim grounded; ABSTAINED = says the sources don't cover it, or a partial-but-accurate answer; WRONG = fabricated or contradicted facts.
rows.raw:
The i.MX 93 handles UART communication through the LPUART (Low Power Universal Asynchronous Receiver/Transmitter) peripheral. Specifically, the reference manual mentions that the LPUART peripheral is available on the i.MX 93. The IP block that routes its pins is the IOMUXC (I/O Multiplexing Controller).

The IOMUXC allows you to configure the multiplexing of the I/O pads. For the LPUART, you can select between different modes, such as `ALT0` for GPIO, `ALT2` for LPUART_TX, and `ALT4` for LPSPI. Here’s an example of how you might select the `ALT2` mode for LPUART7_TX:

```
010b - Select mux mode: ALT2 mux port: LPUART7_TX of instance: imx95_wakeupmix_top
```

This means you would set the MUX_MODE field to `010b` to route the LPUART7_TX pin to the LPUART peripheral.

For a specific pin like GPIO_IO36, you can also force the input path regardless of the MUX_MODE functionality using the SION (Software Input On) field:

```
4 - SION Software Input On Field. Force the selected mux mode Input path no matter of MUX_MODE functionality.
```

If you need to configure a specific pin for LPUART, you would use the appropriate SW_MUX_CTL_PAD register to set the MUX_MODE and SION fields as needed.

CORRECT = accurate answer, every claim grounded; ABSTAINED = says the sources don't cover it, or a partial-but-accurate answer; WRONG = fabricated or contradicted facts.
rows.raw:
On the i.MX 93, the LPUART (Low Power Universal Asynchronous Receiver/Transmitter) peripheral handles UART functionality. Specifically, the LPUART can be routed through the IOMUXC (I/O Multiplex Control) block to route its pins.

For example, the LPUART7_TX pin can be configured using the IOMUXC by selecting one of the available modes. The excerpt provided gives examples of how to configure the LPUART7_TX pin:

- `010b` - Selects `ALT2` mux port: `LPUART7_TX` of instance: `imx95_wakeupmix_top`

This configuration is done by setting the appropriate bits in the IOMUXC control registers. You would need to refer to the specific section of the i.MX 93 reference manual that discusses the IOMUXC and LPUART configurations for more detailed instructions on how to set up the pin routing.

rows.raw:
The i.MX 93 handles UART (Universal Asynchronous Receiver/Transmitter) through the LPUART (Low Power Universal Asynchronous Receiver/Transmitter) peripheral. Specifically, the LPUART peripheral on the i.MX 93 can be used for UART communication.

Regarding the IP block that routes its pins, the LPUART peripheral can be configured to use various pins depending on the specific pin multiplexing configuration (IOMUX) settings. For example, based on the provided excerpts, the LPUART7_TX pin can be configured using the `ALT2` mode, which routes to the `LPUART7_TX` of the `imx95_wakeupmix_top` instance.

To configure which pins the LPUART peripheral uses, you would typically use the IOMUXC (IOMUX Control) module. The exact configuration would involve setting the appropriate MUX modes and possibly the SION (Software Input On) bit if you want to force a specific input path regardless of the MUX mode setting.

For instance, to configure the `GPIO_IO36` pin for LPUART7_TX, you would use a register like `SW_MUX_CTL_PAD_GPIO_IO36` to set the MUX mode to `ALT2` and potentially set the SION bit if necessary.

If you need a specific configuration or further details on how to set up the LPUART peripheral with a particular set of pins, please provide more details or ask a specific question, and I can help guide you through the exact steps.

claims: The i.MX 93 handles UART (Universal Asynchronous Receiver/Transmitter) through the LPUART (Low Power Universal Asynchronous Receiver/Transmitter) peripheral.
Specifically, the LPUART peripheral on the i.MX 93 can be used for UART communication.
Regarding the IP block that routes its pins, the LPUART peripheral can be configured to use various pins depending on the specific pin multiplexing configuration (IOMUX) settings.
For example, based on the provided excerpts, the LPUART7_TX pin can be configured using the `ALT2` mode, which routes to the `LPUART7_TX` of the `imx95_wakeupmix_top` instance.
To configure which pins the LPUART peripheral uses, you would typically use the IOMUXC (IOMUX Control) module.
For instance, to configure the `GPIO_IO36` pin for LPUART7_TX, you would use a register like `SW_MUX_CTL_PAD_GPIO_IO36` to set the MUX mode to `ALT2` and potentially set the SION bit if necessary.

rows.prompt: What Arm cores does the i.MX 93 application processor include?
rows.rubric: Answer this knowledge-base question: 'What Arm cores does the i.MX 93 application processor include?'. Reference facts (may be incomplete or stale — verify against the SOURCE CONTEXT): ['Cortex-A55', 'Cortex-M33']. CORRECT = accurate answer, every claim grounded; ABSTAINED = says the sources don't cover it, or a partial-but-accurate answer; WRONG = fabricated or contradicted facts.
rows.raw:
The i.MX 93 application processor includes two main Arm cores:

1. **Cortex-A55 Core**: This is a 64-bit, dual-core processor operating up to 1.7 GHz. It features:
   - 32 KB L1 Instruction Cache
   - 32 KB L1 Data Cache
   - 64 KB per-core L2 cache
   - Media Processing Engine (MPE) with Arm Neon technology
   - Floating Point Unit (FPU) with support of the Arm VFPv4-D16 architecture
   - 256 KB cluster L3 cache

2. **Cortex-M33 Core**: This is a 32-bit core operating up to 250 MHz. It includes:
   - Support for FPU
   - Support for MPU
   - Support for NVIC
   - Support for FPB
   - Support for DWT and ITM
   - Two-way set-associative 16 KB System Cache with parity support
   - Two-way set-associative 16 KB Code Cache with parity support
   - 256 KB tightly coupled memory (TCM)

These cores work together to provide a balance of performance and energy efficiency, suitable for a wide range of applications from automotive to industrial and consumer IoT markets.

[1] FACT SHEET i.MX 93 APPLICATIONS PROCESSOR FAMILY i.MX 93 applications processors deliver efficient machine learning (ML) acceleration, energy flex architecture and state-of-the-art security to support energy-efficient edge computing. i.MX 93 processors offer fast and efficient ML inferencing along with a rich set of peripherals and high-performance application cores for automotive, industrial and consumer IoT market segments. TARGET APPLICATIONS • Automotive: domain controller compute off-load engine, driver monitoring system, audio, speech recognition, cost-effective gateway • Industrial Automation: gateways, remote I/O controllers, industrial scanners, HMI, machine vision • Building Control and Energy: energy meters, EV charging • Smart Home: home security hub, smart doorbell, smart lock, smart thermostat, AV receivers • Smart City: smart lighting, safety and security, traffic control PERFORMANCE COMPUTE ENGINE The i.MX 93 applications processors are the first in the i.MX portfolio to integrate the scalable Arm® Cortex®-A55 core, bringing best-in-class performance and energy efficiency to Linux-based edge applications. Based on Arm’s DynamIQ technology, the A55 core features the latest Armv8-A architecture extensions with dedicated instructions to accelerate machine learning (ML). NEURAL PROCESSING UNIT (NPU) The i.MX 93 family marks the industry’s first implementation of the Arm® Ethos™-U65 microNPU. A dedicated neural processing unit (NPU), Ethos-U65 delivers a combination of performance and efficiency with an optimized footprint that enables developers to create high-performance, cost- effective and energy-efficient ML applications. BUILT-IN MCU A 250 MHz Arm® Cortex®-M33 processor performs time- critical real-time compute and control. It can eliminate the need for an external microcontroller in the system design. The integrated Cortex-M33 core associated with the CAN FD interfaces provides a robust local control network for industrial applications. Additionally, the built-in Arm Cortex M33 in conjunction with the NPU can be used for low-power wake-word detection. i.MX 93 APPLICATIONS PROCESSOR FAMILY  [url] 2 CAMERA INTERFACES AND IMAGE PROCESSING The i.MX 93 family contains MIPI-CSI and parallel image sensor interfaces along with the NPU to support both monochrome and RGB (color) vision applications. The application processor offers a 2-lane MIPI-CSI camera interface capable of supporting 1080-p60 resolution and enables direct connection to external camera module and ISP. The application processors offer capabilities including down scaling, color space conversion, de-interlacing, alpha insertion, cropping and rotation of images for machine vision and other ML-related applications. DISPLAY AND MULTIMEDIA The i.MX 93 applications processors contain a 4-lane MIPI-DSI capable of supporting 1080p60 resolution, a 4-lane LVDS and parallel display interfaces capable of 720p60 resolution. Additionally, it features a high-efficiency pixel pipeline to perform 2D graphics processing to realize cost-effective GUI solutions. It is capable of image rotation (90°, 180°, 270°), image resize, color space conversion, multiple pixel format support (RGB, YUV444, YUV422, YUV420, YUV400) and standard 2D-DMA operations. SYSTEM SECURITY The i.MX 93 family implements security via NXP’s EdgeLock® secure enclave, a preconfigured, self-managed and autonomous security subsystem.

1. **Cortex-A55 Core**: This is a 64-bit, dual-core processor operating up to 1.7 GHz. It features:
   - 32 KB L1 Instruction Cache
   - 32 KB L1 Data Cache
   - 64 KB per-core L2 cache
   - Media Processing Engine (MPE) with Arm Neon technology
   - Floating Point Unit (FPU) with support of the Arm VFPv4-D16 architecture
   - 256 KB cluster L3 cache

2. **Cortex-M33 Core**: This is a 32-bit core operating up to 250 MHz. It includes:
   - Support for FPU
   - Support for MPU
   - Support for NVIC
   - Support for FPB
   - Support for DWT and ITM
   - Two-way set-associative 16 KB System Cache with parity support
   - Two-way set-associative 16 KB Code Cache with parity support
   - 256 KB tightly coupled memory (TCM)

These cores work together to provide a balance of performance and energy efficiency, suitable for a wide range of applications from automotive to industrial and consumer IoT markets.

The i.MX 93 application processor includes two Arm cores:

1. **Cortex-A55**: This is a high-performance, energy-efficient CPU core. In the i.MX 93, it operates up to 1.7 GHz and features:
   - 32 KB L1 Instruction Cache
   - 32 KB L1 Data Cache
   - 64 KB per-core L2 cache
   - Media Processing Engine (MPE) with Arm Neon technology
   - Floating Point Unit (FPU) with support of the Arm VFPv4-D16 architecture
   - 256 KB cluster L3 cache

2. **Cortex-M33**: This is a low-power CPU core used for monitoring and control tasks. In the i.MX 93, it operates up to 250 MHz and includes:
   - Support for FPU
   - Support for MPU, NVIC, FPB, DWT, and ITM
   - Two-way set-associative 16 KB System Cache with parity support
   - Two-way set-associative 16 KB Code Cache with parity support
   - 256 KB tightly coupled memory (TCM)

These cores are designed to provide a balance between performance and energy efficiency, suitable for a wide range of applications from automotive to industrial and consumer IoT segments.

[1] FACT SHEET i.MX 93 APPLICATIONS PROCESSOR FAMILY i.MX 93 applications processors deliver efficient machine learning (ML) acceleration, energy flex architecture and state-of-the-art security to support energy-efficient edge computing. i.MX 93 processors offer fast and efficient ML inferencing along with a rich set of peripherals and high-performance application cores for automotive, industrial and consumer IoT market segments. TARGET APPLICATIONS • Automotive: domain controller compute off-load engine, driver monitoring system, audio, speech recognition, cost-effective gateway • Industrial Automation: gateways, remote I/O controllers, industrial scanners, HMI, machine vision • Building Control and Energy: energy meters, EV charging • Smart Home: home security hub, smart doorbell, smart lock, smart thermostat, AV receivers • Smart City: smart lighting, safety and security, traffic control PERFORMANCE COMPUTE ENGINE The i.MX 93 applications processors are the first in the i.MX portfolio to integrate the scalable Arm® Cortex®-A55 core, bringing best-in-class performance and energy efficiency to Linux-based edge applications. Based on Arm’s DynamIQ technology, the A55 core features the latest Armv8-A architecture extensions with dedicated instructions to accelerate machine learning (ML). NEURAL PROCESSING UNIT (NPU) The i.MX 93 family marks the industry’s first implementation of the Arm® Ethos™-U65 microNPU. A dedicated neural processing unit (NPU), Ethos-U65 delivers a combination of performance and efficiency with an optimized footprint that enables developers to create high-performance, cost- effective and energy-efficient ML applications. BUILT-IN MCU A 250 MHz Arm® Cortex®-M33 processor performs time- critical real-time compute and control. It can eliminate the need for an external microcontroller in the system design. The integrated Cortex-M33 core associated with the CAN FD interfaces provides a robust local control network for industrial applications. Additionally, the built-in Arm Cortex M33 in conjunction with the NPU can be used for low-power wake-word detection. i.MX 93 APPLICATIONS PROCESSOR FAMILY  [url] 2 CAMERA INTERFACES AND IMAGE PROCESSING The i.MX 93 family contains MIPI-CSI and parallel image sensor interfaces along with the NPU to support both monochrome and RGB (color) vision applications. The application processor offers a 2-lane MIPI-CSI camera interface capable of supporting 1080-p60 resolution and enables direct connection to external camera module and ISP. The application processors offer capabilities including down scaling, color space conversion, de-interlacing, alpha insertion, cropping and rotation of images for machine vision and other ML-related applications. DISPLAY AND MULTIMEDIA The i.MX 93 applications processors contain a 4-lane MIPI-DSI capable of supporting 1080p60 resolution, a 4-lane LVDS and parallel display interfaces capable of 720p60 resolution. Additionally, it features a high-efficiency pixel pipeline to perform 2D graphics processing to realize cost-effective GUI solutions. It is capable of image rotation (90°, 180°, 270°), image resize, color space conversion, multiple pixel format support (RGB, YUV444, YUV422, YUV420, YUV400) and standard 2D-DMA operations. SYSTEM SECURITY The i.MX 93 family implements security via NXP’s EdgeLock® secure enclave, a preconfigured, self-managed and autonomous security subsystem.

rows.raw:
The i.MX 93 application processor includes the following Arm cores:

- **Cortex-A55**: Two Cortex-A55 processors operating up to 1.7 GHz. Each Cortex-A55 core has the following characteristics:
  - 32 KB L1 Instruction Cache
  - 32 KB L1 Data Cache
  - 64 KB per-core L2 cache
  - Media Processing Engine (MPE) with Arm Neon technology
  - Floating Point Unit (FPU) supporting the Arm VFPv4-D16 architecture
  - 256 KB cluster L3 cache

- **Cortex-M33**: A Cortex-M33 core operating up to 250 MHz. This core has the following features:
  - Support for FPU
  - Support for MPU (Memory Protection Unit)
  - Support for NVIC (Nested Vectored Interrupt Controller)
  - Support for FPB (Flash Patch Buffer)
  - Support for DWT (Data Watchpoint and Trace) and ITM (Instrumentation Trace Macrocell)
  - Two-way set-associative 16 KB System Cache with parity support
  - Two-way set-associative 16 KB Code Cache with parity support
  - 256 KB tightly coupled memory (TCM)

The Cortex-A55 cores are designed for high-performance applications, while the Cortex-M33 core is optimized for low-power, real-time tasks and IoT applications.
rows.context:
[1] FACT SHEET i.MX 93 APPLICATIONS PROCESSOR FAMILY i.MX 93 applications processors deliver efficient machine learning (ML) acceleration, energy flex architecture and state-of-the-art security to support energy-efficient edge computing. i.MX 93 processors offer fast and efficient ML inferencing along with a rich set of peripherals and high-performance application cores for automotive, industrial and consumer IoT market segments. TARGET APPLICATIONS • Automotive: domain controller compute off-load engine, driver monitoring system, audio, speech recognition, cost-effective gateway • Industrial Automation: gateways, remote I/O controllers, industrial scanners, HMI, machine vision • Building Control and Energy: energy meters, EV charging • Smart Home: home security hub, smart doorbell, smart lock, smart thermostat, AV receivers • Smart City: smart lighting, safety and security, traffic control PERFORMANCE COMPUTE ENGINE The i.MX 93 applications processors are the first in the i.MX portfolio to integrate the scalable Arm® Cortex®-A55 core, bringing best-in-class performance and energy efficiency to Linux-based edge applications. Based on Arm’s DynamIQ technology, the A55 core features the latest Armv8-A architecture extensions with dedicated instructions to accelerate machine learning (ML). NEURAL PROCESSING UNIT (NPU) The i.MX 93 family marks the industry’s first implementation of the Arm® Ethos™-U65 microNPU. A dedicated neural processing unit (NPU), Ethos-U65 delivers a combination of performance and efficiency with an optimized footprint that enables developers to create high-performance, cost- effective and energy-efficient ML applications. BUILT-IN MCU A 250 MHz Arm® Cortex®-M33 processor performs time- critical real-time compute and control. It can eliminate the need for an external microcontroller in the system design. The integrated Cortex-M33 core associated with the CAN FD interfaces provides a robust local control network for industrial applications. Additionally, the built-in Arm Cortex M33 in conjunction with the NPU can be used for low-power wake-word detection. i.MX 93 APPLICATIONS PROCESSOR FAMILY  [url] 2 CAMERA INTERFACES AND IMAGE PROCESSING The i.MX 93 family contains MIPI-CSI and parallel image sensor interfaces along with the NPU to support both monochrome and RGB (color) vision applications. The application processor offers a 2-lane MIPI-CSI camera interface capable of supporting 1080-p60 resolution and enables direct connection to external camera module and ISP. The application processors offer capabilities including down scaling, color space conversion, de-interlacing, alpha insertion, cropping and rotation of images for machine vision and other ML-related applications. DISPLAY AND MULTIMEDIA The i.MX 93 applications processors contain a 4-lane MIPI-DSI capable of supporting 1080p60 resolution, a 4-lane LVDS and parallel display interfaces capable of 720p60 resolution. Additionally, it features a high-efficiency pixel pipeline to perform 2D graphics processing to realize cost-effective GUI solutions. It is capable of image rotation (90°, 180°, 270°), image resize, color space conversion, multiple pixel format support (RGB, YUV444, YUV422, YUV420, YUV400) and standard 2D-DMA operations. SYSTEM SECURITY The i.MX 93 family implements security via NXP’s EdgeLock® secure enclave, a preconfigured, self-managed and autonomous security subsystem.

rows.context:
[1] [...] Solutions for automotive eCockpits. Explore NXP i.MX applications processors for eCockpit Infotainment.

Altia and NXP Semiconductors offer a powerful combination of technologies to build integrated cockpit designs for automotive applications. Together, we are delivering immersive in-vehicle experiences. Our latest eCockpit demo—housed in a production Mercedes and driven by two NXP i.MX 8QuadMax applications processors—delivers a seamless user experience for the driver and passenger. The graphics, powered by Altia HMI development software, reflect a cohesive look and feel that helps improve the user experience. The C source code generated by Altia DeepScreen optimizes the capabilities of the i.MX 8 to ensure the best use of the vehicle’s available power.
Building Advanced HMIs with Altia and NXP

The Connected eCockpit was conceived and designed by Altia’s Professional Engineering Services team and created using Altia Design 13. Altia’s HMI software allows technical artists, designers and engineers the ability to build high-performance HMIs without hand-coding graphics, resulting in rapid time to production. The teams were able to leverage assets from 2D and 3D design tools, making artwork import easy. Altia DeepScreen code generator then outputs the code running on the i.MX 8QuadMax. [1] [...] Solutions for automotive eCockpits. Explore NXP i.MX applications processors for eCockpit Infotainment.

Altia and NXP Semiconductors offer a powerful combination of technologies to build integrated cockpit designs for automotive applications. Together, we are delivering immersive in-vehicle experiences. Our latest eCockpit demo—housed in a production Mercedes and driven by two NXP i.MX 8QuadMax applications processors—delivers a seamless user experience for the driver and passenger. The graphics, powered by Altia HMI development software, reflect a cohesive look and feel that helps improve the user experience. The C source code generated by Altia DeepScreen optimizes the capabilities of the i.MX 8 to ensure the best use of the vehicle’s available power.
Building Advanced HMIs with Altia and NXP

The Connected eCockpit was conceived and designed by Altia’s Professional Engineering Services team and created using Altia Design 13. Altia’s HMI software allows technical artists, designers and engineers the ability to build high-performance HMIs without hand-coding graphics, resulting in rapid time to production. The teams were able to leverage assets from 2D and 3D design tools, making artwork import easy. Altia DeepScreen code generator then outputs the code running on the i.MX 8QuadMax. DeepScreen supports a wide range of NXP platforms – from low-power MCUs to high-performance applications processors. This includes i.MX 8, i.MX 6, and i.MX crossover MCUs including i.MX RT1052, i.MX RT1062, i.MX RT1170, S32V, MAC57D5xx, MPC5645S, MPC5606S, i.MX28, i.MX53, LPC1788 and VFxxx.

NXP supplies the i.MX 8 platform, an applications processor which offers the processing power to drive full dashboard HMIs at top performance. The eCockpit includes two NXP i.MX 8 QuadMax SoCs, which come equipped with two ARM® Cortex®-A72 cores, four ARM Cortex-A53 cores, two Arm Cortex-M4F cores plus 64-bit LPDDR4/DDR4 DRAM.
Futuristic Features Realized for CES 2022

The Connected eCockpit demonstrates unified integration of HMI elements between two screens— a 12.3” (1920x720) instrument cluster and 28” (3840x720) passenger display—with state-of-the-art pillar-to-pillar graphics powered by Altia and two NXP i.MX 8QuadMax applications processors. The eCockpit uses multiple OS architectures with Linux® in the instrument cluster and Android in the 4K passenger display.
Altia eCockpit Displays

The eCockpit design follows a modern interaction paradigm inspired by mobile phones. This was driven in part by Jakobs Law –meaning that users expect new interfaces to behave like the ones they already know. This unified HMI user experience embraces automotive tech considerations including EV readouts, advanced ADAS, reconfigurable layout and data streaming. Altia designers and developers created a UX for drivers and passengers across the cockpit displays, serving up real-time advanced 3D throughout.
Altia 12.3” Instrument Cluster

The 12.3” instrument cluster demonstrates intuitive design elements to inform EV drivers. For example, safety particles appear above the speed readout and accumulate with good driving, providing a gamified experience to keep drivers safe and engaged. A power histogram visualizes the vehicle’s power output in real-time. Additionally, active following distance assist in the center of the cluster gives the driver helpful feedback to set a safe follow distance from the car in front of the vehicle.
Altia 28” (3840x720) passenger display

rows.raw:
Based on the information provided in the excerpts, the maximum number of standard ID filter elements supported by the i.MX 93 Applications Processor's FlexCAN controller can be determined from the tables:

For `NEXIF = 0` (no extended ID filters):
- The maximum number of standard ID filter elements is 128.

For `NEXIF > 0` (when extended ID filters are used), the number of standard ID filter elements decreases as the number of extended ID filter elements increases. The table shows that as `NFE` (number of enhanced RX FIFO filter elements) increases, the number of standard ID filter elements decreases until it reaches a minimum of 2.

Specifically:
- For `NFE = 64`, the number of standard ID filter elements is 0.
- For `NFE = 63`, the number of standard ID filter elements is 2.
- As `NFE` decreases further, the number of standard ID filter elements increases up to a maximum of 128 when `NFE` is 0.

Therefore, the maximum number of standard ID filter elements supported by the i.MX 93 Applications Processor's FlexCAN controller is 128.

rows.raw: The size of the L1 data cache per core in the Arm Cortex-A55 on the i.MX 93 is 32 kByte.
rows.context:
[1] — 32 kByte L1 Data Cache — 64 kByte per-core L2 cache — Media Processing Engine (MPE) with NEON technology supporting the Advanced Single Instruction Multiple Data architecture — Floating Point Unit (FPU) with support of the VFPv4-D16 architecture • Support of 64-bit Arm v8.2-A architecture • 256 kByte cluster L3 cache • Various components composing the CoreSightTM debug and trace technology, such as ETM, CTM and CTI • The DynamIQ Shared Unit (DSU) shared between cores, includes Snoop Control Unit (SCU), L3 cache, ACE interface, etc. 12.2 Functional Description The sections below discuss the high-level overview of the Arm Cortex-A55 Platform components. 12.2.1 Arm Cortex-A55 MPCore Processor The Arm Cortex-A55 processor implements the Armv8-A architecture. the A55 complex has 2. Each core has a 32 kByte L1 Instruction Cache, a 32 kByte L1 Data Cache and a 64 kByte per-core L2 cache. Each core also has a Media Processing Engine (MPE) with NEON technology supporting the Advanced Single Instruction Multiple Data architecture and a Floating Point Unit (FPU) with support of the VFPv4-D16 architecture. 12.2.2 DynamIQ Shared Unit (DSU) The DynamIQ Shared Unit (DSU) is the portion of the A55 complex that is shared between the cores. The DSU includes the Snoop Control Unit (SCU), L3 cache, etc. The SCU arbitrates between the cores requesting L3 cache access. 12.2.3 Advanced SIMD (NEON) The Cortex-A55 processor supports the Advanced SIMD and Scalar Floating-point instructions. See Arm Cortex-A55 documentation for more information. 12.2.4 Atomic Instructions The Arm Cortex-A55 Core Technical Reference Manual mentions that atomics are supported to cacheable memory but requires a coherent interconnect to support atomics to device or non-cacheable memory. This product does not support such a coherent interconnect. If such an atomic instruction is executed when the interconnect does not support them, it will result in a synchronous Data Abort (for load atomics) or an asynchronous Data Abort (for store atomics) 12.2.5 Debug The Cortex-A55 platform includes the debug and trace sub-modules. The debug interface is connected to the DAP and CoreSight debug modules in the SoC to allow debug through JTAG interface. See the System Debug chapter for more information about the A55 Platform debug components, such as ETM, CTI and CTM. 12.2.6 Clocking The Cortex-A55 platform takes in the following clocks, all of which may be fully asynchronous to each other. NXP Semiconductors ARM Cortex A55 i.MX 93 Applications Processor Reference Manual, Rev. 5, 05/2024 Reference Manual General Business Information 293 / 5652  Table 62. A55 Clocks A55 Platform Clock Name Source Frequency (Nominal Voltage) Description PERIPHCLK CCM: Arm_a55_periphclk_root 333MHz Timers, clock and power management logic in Cortex-A55 platform. rows.context:
[1] — 32 kByte L1 Data Cache — 64 kByte per-core L2 cache — Media Processing Engine (MPE) with NEON technology supporting the Advanced Single Instruction Multiple Data architecture — Floating Point Unit (FPU) with support of the VFPv4-D16 architecture • Support of 64-bit Arm v8.2-A architecture • 256 kByte cluster L3 cache • Various components composing the CoreSightTM debug and trace technology, such as ETM, CTM and CTI • The DynamIQ Shared Unit (DSU) shared between cores, includes Snoop Control Unit (SCU), L3 cache, ACE interface, etc. 12.2 Functional Description The sections below discuss the high-level overview of the Arm Cortex-A55 Platform components. 12.2.1 Arm Cortex-A55 MPCore Processor The Arm Cortex-A55 processor implements the Armv8-A architecture. the A55 complex has 2. Each core has a 32 kByte L1 Instruction Cache, a 32 kByte L1 Data Cache and a 64 kByte per-core L2 cache. Each core also has a Media Processing Engine (MPE) with NEON technology supporting the Advanced Single Instruction Multiple Data architecture and a Floating Point Unit (FPU) with support of the VFPv4-D16 architecture. 12.2.2 DynamIQ Shared Unit (DSU) The DynamIQ Shared Unit (DSU) is the portion of the A55 complex that is shared between the cores. The DSU includes the Snoop Control Unit (SCU), L3 cache, etc. The SCU arbitrates between the cores requesting L3 cache access. 12.2.3 Advanced SIMD (NEON) The Cortex-A55 processor supports the Advanced SIMD and Scalar Floating-point instructions. See Arm Cortex-A55 documentation for more information. 12.2.4 Atomic Instructions The Arm Cortex-A55 Core Technical Reference Manual mentions that atomics are supported to cacheable memory but requires a coherent interconnect to support atomics to device or non-cacheable memory. This product does not support such a coherent interconnect. If such an atomic instruction is executed when the interconnect does not support them, it will result in a synchronous Data Abort (for load atomics) or an asynchronous Data Abort (for store atomics) 12.2.5 Debug The Cortex-A55 platform includes the debug and trace sub-modules. The debug interface is connected to the DAP and CoreSight debug modules in the SoC to allow debug through JTAG interface. See the System Debug chapter for more information about the A55 Platform debug components, such as ETM, CTI and CTM. 12.2.6 Clocking The Cortex-A55 platform takes in the following clocks, all of which may be fully asynchronous to each other. Each core has a 32 kByte L1 Instruction Cache, a 32 kByte L1 Data Cache and a 64 kByte per-core L2 cache. Each core also has a Media Processing Engine (MPE) with NEON technology supporting the Advanced Single Instruction Multiple Data architecture and a Floating Point Unit (FPU) with support of the VFPv4-D16 architecture. 12.2.2 DynamIQ Shared Unit (DSU) The DynamIQ Shared Unit (DSU) is the portion of the A55 complex that is shared between the cores. The DSU includes the Snoop Control Unit (SCU), L3 cache, etc. The SCU arbitrates between the cores requesting L3 cache access. 12.2.3 Advanced SIMD (NEON) The Cortex-A55 processor supports the Advanced SIMD and Scalar Floating-point instructions. See Arm Cortex-A55 documentation for more information. 12.2.4 Atomic Instructions The Arm Cortex-A55 Core Technical Reference Manual mentions that atomics are supported to cacheable memory but requires a coherent interconnect to support atomics to device or non-cacheable memory. This product does not support such a coherent interconnect. If such an atomic instruction is executed when the interconnect does not support them, it will result in a synchronous Data Abort (for load atomics) or an asynchronous Data Abort (for store atomics) 12.2.5 Debug The Cortex-A55 platform includes the debug and trace sub-modules. The debug interface is connected to the DAP and CoreSight debug modules in the SoC to allow debug through JTAG interface. See the System Debug chapter for more information about the A55 Platform debug components, such as ETM, CTI and CTM. 12.2.6 Clocking The Cortex-A55 platform takes in the following clocks, all of which may be fully asynchronous to each other. The DSU includes the Snoop Control Unit (SCU), L3 cache, etc. The SCU arbitrates between the cores requesting L3 cache access. 12.2.3 Advanced SIMD (NEON) The Cortex-A55 processor supports the Advanced SIMD and Scalar Floating-point instructions. See Arm Cortex-A55 documentation for more information. 12.2.4 Atomic Instructions The Arm Cortex-A55 Core Technical Reference Manual mentions that atomics are supported to cacheable memory but requires a coherent interconnect to support atomics to device or non-cacheable memory. This product does not support such a coherent interconnect. If such an atomic instruction is executed when the interconnect does not support them, it will result in a synchronous Data Abort (for load atomics) or an asynchronous Data Abort (for store atomics) 12.2.5 Debug The Cortex-A55 platform includes the debug and trace sub-modules. The debug interface is connected to the DAP and CoreSight debug modules in the SoC to allow debug through JTAG interface. See the System Debug chapter for more information about the A55 Platform debug components, such as ETM, CTI and CTM. 12.2.6 Clocking The Cortex-A55 platform takes in the following clocks, all of which may be fully asynchronous to each other. MIPI CSI-2
MIPI CSI-2 Interface
Key features of MIPI CSI-2 controller are listed as following:
 • Complaint with MIPI CSI-2 specification v1.3 and MIPI D-PHY 
specification v1.2
 • Support up to 2 Rx data lanes (plus 1 Rx clock lane)
 • MIPI CSI-2 supports:
– Pixel clock up to 200 MHz (at both nominal and overdrive 
voltage)
– Up to approximately 150 Mpixel/s supported
– 80 Mbps to 1.5 Gbps per lane data rate in high speed operation
 • Support 10 Mbps data rate in low power operation

[Page 11 Tables]
i.MX 93 Application Processors Data Sheet for Commercial Products, Rev. 3, 12/2023

MIPI DSI
MIPI DSI Interface
Key features of MIPI DSI controller are listed as following:
 • Support one 4-lane MIPI DSI display with pixels from the LCDIF
 • Compliant to MIPI DSI specification v1.2 and MIPI D-PHY 
specification v1.2
 • The maximum pixel clock is 200 MHz and active pixel rate of 140 
Mpixel/s with 24-bit RGB. This includes resolutions such as 
1080p60 or 1920x1200p60. 
 • The maximum data rate per lane is 1.5 Gbps.

OCRAM
On-Chip Memory controller
The On-Chip Memory controller (OCRAM) module is designed as an 
interface between the system’s AXI bus and the internal (on-chip) 
SRAM memory module.
In i.MX 93 processors, 640 KB OCRAM is used for
 • 256 KB for resident Cortex-A Trusted Execution Environment
 • 384 Kbytes for ML NPU
 • All 640 Kbytes can be accessed by software when the NPU ML 
Accelerator is not used.

Cortex®-A55 MPCore platform
Two Cortex®-A55 processors operating up to 1.7 GHz

256 KB cluster L3 cache

 • Support FPU

 • Support NVIC
 • Support FPB
 • Support DWT and ITM
 • Two-way set-associative 16 KB System Cache with parity support
 • Two-way set-associative 16 KB Code Cache with parity support
 • 256 KB tightly coupled memory (TCM)

Neural Processing Unit (NPU)
 Neural Network performance (256 MACs operating up to 1.0 GHz and 2 OPS/MAC)
 • NPU targets 8-bit and 16-bit integer RNN
 • Handles 8-bit weights

On-chip memory
Boot ROM (256 KB) for Cortex®-A55

Boot ROM (256 KB) for Cortex®-M33

 • One SDXC (4-bit, no eMMC5.1, with extended capacity)

rows.raw:
The maximum voltage allowed for VDD_USB_3P3 on the i.MX 93 is 3.45 V. This can be found in the operating ranges section of the i.MX 93 Application Processors Data Sheets for various temperature ranges (Commercial, Industrial, Extended Industrial, and Automotive). The specific excerpt from the datasheet states:

- VDD_USB_3P3: 3.069 V to 3.45 V

This range ensures the proper operation of the USB PHY circuits powered by VDD_USB_3P3.

[1] The i.MX 93 Applications Processor is a new CPU generation with many advantages High flexibility based on the latest technologies WHITEPAPER  WHITEPAPER | The i.MX 93 Applications Processor is a new CPU generation with many advantages 2 How does the i.MX 93 processor fit into the i.MX 9 series? 3 Module Designs i.MX 93 processor 5 Mainboard Design 7 Available modules/mainboards of the i.MX 93 processor from TQ 15 Additional Information 18 Content  WHITEPAPER | The i.MX 93 Applications Processor is a new CPU generation with many advantages 3 The i.MX 93 processor How does the i.MX 93 processor fit into the i.MX 9 series? The i.MX 93 processor uses the Cortex A55 core with clock speeds up to 1.7 GHz. The Cortex-A55 processor core uses DynamIQ technology (the successor to Arm‘s big.LITTLE concept) and features the latest enhancements to the ARMv8.2-A architecture with a dedicated instruc­ tion set to accelerate machine learning (ML) models. According to NXP, the i.MX 93 processor is the first in the industry to implement ARM‘s Ethos-U65 microNPU with a performance of 256 MACs/cycle. The Ethos-U65 offers a very good combination of performance and efficiency in a very small size, enabling developers to realize high- performance, low-cost and energy-efficient ML applications. The i.MX 93 processor also contains a 250 MHz Cortex-M33 processor core for time-critical real-time computation and control and the EdgeLock Secure Enclave for providing the security functions. The memory interface is 16-bit wide and supports LPDDR4 and LPDDR4X with internal ECC support. In addition to up to 7 x I²S audio interfaces and 8-channel PDM microphone inputs, the processor offers extensive interfaces: CAN-FD, UARTs, SPI, QSPI, I²C and SDIO. Extensive security functions are also implemented. With the i.MX 93 processor, NXP offers a price- and feature-optimized CPU from the i.MX 9 series. Next to the i.MX 91 processor, the i.MX 93 processor is the smallest CPU in the i.MX 9 series and a good alternative to the i.MX 28 processor, i.MX 6UL/i.MX 6ULL processor for new designs. The main difference between this CPU and its pre­ decessors in terms of graphics and video interfaces is the addition of 24-bit RGB, MIPI-DSI and LVDS interfaces. A total of four CPU variants are available, from single-core to dual-core with/without NPU and qualified to operate at different temperature range The most important interfaces are available as follows: • 1x MIPI DSI 4 Lanes (display serial interface) • 1x LVDS 4 Lanes • 1x MIPI CSI 2 Lanes (camera sensor interface) • 3x SDIO supporting SD/eMMC/Wi-Fi • 2x USB 2.0 • 2x Gigabit Ethernet (1x TSN) • 2x CAN-FD • 8x UART, 8x I²C, 8x SPI, 7x I²S • 1x QSPI • 1x 4-ch, 12-bit ADC A serial camera interface (MIPI-CSI) allows a camera to be connected directly to the CPU and supports its use in digital imaging applications. The i.MX 93 processor is based on the same Arm Core architecture as the entire i.MX 9 series.

This core uses DynamIQ technology, the successor to Arm‘s big.LITTLE concept, and features the latest extensions to the Armv8-A architecture, including a dedicated instruction set for implementing energy-ef- ficient control systems. The „EdgeLock Secure Enclave“ provides further support for the simple implementation of security concepts. The 16-bit memory interface uses LPDDR4 and offers optional internal ECC support. In addition to offering up to four I²S audio interfaces and eight PDM microphone inputs, the processor provides numerous other interfaces. These include CAN-FD, UARTs, SPI, QSPI, I²C, and SDIO. It also has extensive security functions. There are two CPU variants available, which differ mainly in clock frequency. NXP offers the i.MX 91 Processor, an optimized CPU in terms of price and functionality from the i.MX 9 family. The i.MX 91 is the smallest CPU in the i.MX 9 family, alongside the i.MX 93, and it is an excellent alternative to the i.MX 28 and i.MX 6UL/i.MX 6ULL for new designs. Like the rest of the i.MX 9 family, the i.MX 91 is based on the same core architecture. Its main differences are its integrated safety functions, The i.MX 91‘s main interfaces are: • 1x 24-Bit RGB display • 1x 8 Bit RGB camera interface • 3x SDIO/eMMC • 2x USB 2.0 • 2x Gigabit Ethernet (1 x with TSN) • 2x CAN FD • 8x UART, 8x I²C, 8x SPI, 4x I²S • 1x QSPI • 2x FlexIO • 1x Medium quality sound output (Sigma-Delta modulator) network interfaces, and CAN interfaces, including dual Gigabit Ethernet and dual CAN FD. A parallel camera inter- face (8-bit RGB) enables direct connection of a camera to the CPU and supports applications involving basic image processing. This provides a high degree of flexibility in designing a main- board to optimize CPU utilization and ensure maximum efficiency. TQ-Embedded has developed two modules that allow all i.MX 91 and i.MX 93 derivatives to be used in the same design despite CPU differences.

The i.MX 93 processor uses the Cortex A55 core with clock speeds up to 1.7 GHz. The Cortex-A55 processor core uses DynamIQ technology (the successor to Arm‘s big.LITTLE concept) and features the latest enhancements to the ARMv8.2-A architecture with a dedicated instruc­ tion set to accelerate machine learning (ML) models. According to NXP, the i.MX 93 processor is the first in the industry to implement ARM‘s Ethos-U65 microNPU with a performance of 256 MACs/cycle. The Ethos-U65 offers a very good combination of performance and efficiency in a very small size, enabling developers to realize high- performance, low-cost and energy-efficient ML applications. The i.MX 93 processor also contains a 250 MHz Cortex-M33 processor core for time-critical real-time computation and control and the EdgeLock Secure Enclave for providing the security functions. The memory interface is 16-bit wide and supports LPDDR4 and LPDDR4X with internal ECC support. In addition to up to 7 x I²S audio interfaces and 8-channel PDM microphone inputs, the processor offers extensive interfaces: CAN-FD, UARTs, SPI, QSPI, I²C and SDIO. Extensive security functions are also implemented. With the i.MX 93 processor, NXP offers a price- and feature-optimized CPU from the i.MX 9 series. Next to the i.MX 91 processor, the i.MX 93 processor is the smallest CPU in the i.MX 9 series and a good alternative to the i.MX 28 processor, i.MX 6UL/i.MX 6ULL processor for new designs. The main difference between this CPU and its pre­ decessors in terms of graphics and video interfaces is the addition of 24-bit RGB, MIPI-DSI and LVDS interfaces. A total of four CPU variants are available, from single-core to dual-core with/without NPU and qualified to operate at different temperature range The most important interfaces are available as follows: • 1x MIPI DSI 4 Lanes (display serial interface) • 1x LVDS 4 Lanes • 1x MIPI CSI 2 Lanes (camera sensor interface) • 3x SDIO supporting SD/eMMC/Wi-Fi • 2x USB 2.0 • 2x Gigabit Ethernet (1x TSN) • 2x CAN-FD • 8x UART, 8x I²C, 8x SPI, 7x I²S • 1x QSPI • 1x 4-ch, 12-bit ADC A serial camera interface (MIPI-CSI) allows a camera to be connected directly to the CPU and supports its use in digital imaging applications. rows.raw:
The USB 2.0 PHY on the i.MX 93 supports three data transmission rates according to the UTMI+ specification:

- High-Speed (HS): 480 Mbps
- Full-Speed (FS): 12 Mbps
- Low-Speed (LS): 1.5 Mbps

These rates are designed to accommodate a wide range of devices and applications, ensuring compatibility with both newer and older USB devices.

[2] When system software has initiated the charger detection sequence, as described in Initial system conditions, the USBDCD module turns on the IDP_SRC current source and enables the RDM_DWN pulldown resistor. If the data pins have not made contact, the D+ line remains high. After the data pins make contact, the D+ line goes low and debouncing begins. After the D+ line goes low, the module continuously samples the D+ line over the duration of the TDCD_DBNC debounce time interval. By default, TDCD_DBNC is 10 ms, but it can be programmed in the TIMER0[TDCD_DBNC] field. See the description of TIMER0 for details. When it has remained low for the entire interval, the debouncing is complete. However, if the D+ line returns high during the debounce interval, the module waits until the D+ line goes low again to restart the debouncing. This cycle repeats until either of the following happens: • The data pin contact has been successfully debounced (see Success in detecting data pin contact (phase completion)). • A timeout occurs (see Charger detection sequence timeout). 63.3.2.3.2 Success in detecting data pin contact (phase completion) After successfully debouncing the D+ state, the module does the following: • Updates the STATUS register to reflect phase completion (See Table 505 for field values.) • Directly proceeds to the next step in the sequence: detection of a charging port (See Charging port detection.) 63.3.2.4 Charging port detection After it detects that the data pins have made contact, the module waits for a fixed delay of 1 ms, and then attempts to detect whether it is plugged into a charging port. The module connects the following analog units to the USB D+ or D– lines during this phase: • The voltage source VDP_SRC connects to the D+ line • The current sink IDM_SINK connects to the D– line • The voltage comparator connects to the USB D– line, comparing it to the voltage VDAT_REF. After a time of TVDPSRC_ON, the module samples the D– line. The TVDPSRC_ON parameter is programmable and defaults to 40 ms. After sampling the D– line, the module disconnects the voltage source, current sink, and comparator. Therefore, there may be several micro-frames of activity on the port until the host controller evaluates the Suspend bit. The host controller must evaluate the Suspend bit at least every frame boundary. System software can initiate a resume on a selectively suspended port by writing one to the Force Port Resume bit. Software should not attempt to resume a port unless the port reports that it is in the suspended state (see USB_nPORTSC1). If system software sets Force Port Resume bit to one when the port is not in the suspended state, the resulting behavior is undefined. In order to assure proper USB device operation, software must wait for at least 10 ms after a port indicates that it is suspended (Suspend bit is one) before initiating a port resume through the Force Port Resume bit. When Force Port Resume bit is one, the host controller sends resume signaling down the port. System software times the duration of the resume (nominally 20 ms) then sets the Force Port Resume bit to zero. When the host controller receives the write to transition Force Port Resume to zero, it completes the resume sequence as defined in the USB specification, and sets both the Force Port Resume and Suspend bits to zero. Software-initiated port resumes do not affect the Port Change Detect bit in the USB_USBSTS register nor do they cause an interrupt if the Port Change Interrupt Enable bit in the USB_USBINTR register is one. An external USB event may also initiate a resume. The wake events are defined above. When a wake event occurs on a suspended port, the resume signaling is detected by the port and the resume is reflected downstream within 100 μsec. The port's Force Port Resume bit is set to one and the Port Change Detect bit in the USB_USBSTS register is set to one. If the Port Change Interrupt Enable bit in the USB_USBINTR register is one the host controller issues a hardware interrupt. System software observes the resume event on the port, delays a port resume time (nominally 20 ms), then terminates the resume sequence by writing zero to the Force Port Resume bit in the port. The host controller receives the write of zero to Force Port Resume, terminates the resume sequence and sets Force Port Resume and Suspend port bits to zero. Software can determine that the port is enabled (not suspended) by sampling the USB_PORTSC1 register and observing that the Suspend and Force Port Resume bits are zero. Software must ensure that the host controller is running (that is HCHalted bit in the USB_USBSTS register is zero), before terminating a resume by writing zero to a port's Force Port Resume bit. If HCHalted is one when Force Port Resume is set to zero, then SOFs do not occur down the enabled port and the device returns to suspend mode in a maximum of 10 msec. Attached devices must be prepared to suspend at any time they are powered, regardless of if they have been assigned a non-default address, are configured, or neither. [1] When system software has initiated the charger detection sequence, as described in Initial system conditions, the USBDCD module turns on the IDP_SRC current source and enables the RDM_DWN pulldown resistor. If the data pins have not made contact, the D+ line remains high. After the data pins make contact, the D+ line goes low and debouncing begins. After the D+ line goes low, the module continuously samples the D+ line over the duration of the TDCD_DBNC debounce time interval. By default, TDCD_DBNC is 10 ms, but it can be programmed in the TIMER0[TDCD_DBNC] field. See the description of TIMER0 for details. When it has remained low for the entire interval, the debouncing is complete. However, if the D+ line returns high during the debounce interval, the module waits until the D+ line goes low again to restart the debouncing. This cycle repeats until either of the following happens: • The data pin contact has been successfully debounced (see Success in detecting data pin contact (phase completion)). • A timeout occurs (see Charger detection sequence timeout). 63.3.2.3.2 Success in detecting data pin contact (phase completion) After successfully debouncing the D+ state, the module does the following: • Updates the STATUS register to reflect phase completion (See Table 505 for field values.) • Directly proceeds to the next step in the sequence: detection of a charging port (See Charging port detection.) 63.3.2.4 Charging port detection After it detects that the data pins have made contact, the module waits for a fixed delay of 1 ms, and then attempts to detect whether it is plugged into a charging port. The module connects the following analog units to the USB D+ or D– lines during this phase: • The voltage source VDP_SRC connects to the D+ line • The current sink IDM_SINK connects to the D– line • The voltage comparator connects to the USB D– line, comparing it to the voltage VDAT_REF. After a time of TVDPSRC_ON, the module samples the D– line. The TVDPSRC_ON parameter is programmable and defaults to 40 ms. After sampling the D– line, the module disconnects the voltage source, current sink, and comparator. The next steps in the sequence depend on the voltage on the D– line as determined by the voltage comparator. See the following table. Table 500. Sampling D– in the charging port detection phase If the voltage on D- is... Then... See... Below VDAT_REF The port is an SDP that does not support using charging currents above ICFG_MAX. SDP Above VDAT_REF but below VLGC The port is a charging port. Charging port Above VLGC This is an error condition. Error in charging port detection 63.3.2.4.1 SDP As part of the charger detection handshake with a standard USB host, the module does the following without waiting for the interval (TWAIT_AFTER_PRD or TVDPSRC_CON) to elapse: • Updates the STATUS register to reflect that an SDP is detected with SEQ_RES = 01b. See Table 505 for field values. • Sets CONTROL[IF].

[2] [...] Therefore, there may be several micro-frames of activity on the port until the host controller evaluates the Suspend bit. The host controller must evaluate the Suspend bit at least every frame boundary.

Therefore, there may be several micro-frames of activity on the port until the host controller evaluates the Suspend bit. The host controller must evaluate the Suspend bit at least every frame boundary. System software can initiate a resume on a selectively suspended port by writing one to the Force Port Resume bit. Software should not attempt to resume a port unless the port reports that it is in the suspended state (see USB_nPORTSC1). If system software sets Force Port Resume bit to one when the port is not in the suspended state, the resulting behavior is undefined. In order to assure proper USB device operation, software must wait for at least 10 ms after a port indicates that it is suspended (Suspend bit is one) before initiating a port resume through the Force Port Resume bit. When Force Port Resume bit is one, the host controller sends resume signaling down the port. System software times the duration of the resume (nominally 20 ms) then sets the Force Port Resume bit to zero. When the host controller receives the write to transition Force Port Resume to zero, it completes the resume sequence as defined in the USB specification, and sets both the Force Port Resume and Suspend bits to zero. Software-initiated port resumes do not affect the Port Change Detect bit in the USB_USBSTS register nor do they cause an interrupt if the Port Change Interrupt Enable bit in the USB_USBINTR register is one. An external USB event may also initiate a resume. The wake events are defined above. When a wake event occurs on a suspended port, the resume signaling is detected by the port and the resume is reflected downstream within 100 μsec. The port's Force Port Resume bit is set to one and the Port Change Detect bit in the USB_USBSTS register is set to one. If the Port Change Interrupt Enable bit in the USB_USBINTR register is one the host controller issues a hardware interrupt. System software observes the resume event on the port, delays a port resume time (nominally 20 ms), then terminates the resume sequence by writing zero to the Force Port Resume bit in the port. The host controller receives the write of zero to Force Port Resume, terminates the resume sequence and sets Force Port Resume and Suspend port bits to zero. Software can determine that the port is enabled (not suspended) by sampling the USB_PORTSC1 register and observing that the Suspend and Force Port Resume bits are zero. Software must ensure that the host controller is running (that is HCHalted bit in the USB_USBSTS register is zero), before terminating a resume by writing zero to a port's Force Port Resume bit. If HCHalted is one when Force Port Resume is set to zero, then SOFs do not occur down the enabled port and the device returns to suspend mode in a maximum of 10 msec. The table below summarizes the wake-up events.

[3] [...] Cancel all primed status by waiting until all bits in the USB_nENDPTPRIME are 0 and then writing 0xFFFFFFFF to USB_nENDPTFLUSH. Read the reset bit in the USB_nPORTSC1 register and make sure that it is still active.

Cancel all primed status by waiting until all bits in the USB_nENDPTPRIME are 0 and then writing 0xFFFFFFFF to USB_nENDPTFLUSH. Read the reset bit in the USB_nPORTSC1 register and make sure that it is still active. A USB reset will occur for a minimum of 3 ms and the DCD must reach this point in the reset cleanup before end of the reset occurs, otherwise a hardware reset of the device controller is recommended (rare.) • A hardware reset can be performed by writing a one to the device controller reset bit in the USBCMD reset. Note: a hardware reset will cause the device to detach from the bus by clearing the Run/Stop bit. Thus, the DCD must completely re-initialize the device controller after a hardware reset. Free all allocated dTDs because they will no longer be executed by the device controller. If this is the first time the DCD is processing a USB reset event, then it is likely that no dTDs have been allocated. At this time, the DCD may release control back to the OS because no further changes to the device controller are permitted until a Port Change Detect is indicated. After a Port Change Detect, the device has reached the default state and the DCD can read the USB_nPORTSC1 to determine if the device is operating in FS or HS mode. At this time, the device controller has reached normal operating mode and DCD can begin enumeration according to the USB Chapter 9 - Device Framework. The device DCD may use the FS/HS mode information to determine the bandwidth mode of the device. NOTE In some applications, it may not be possible to enable one or more pipes while in FS mode. Beyond the data rate issue, there is no difference in DCD operation between FS and HS modes. 41.3.2.3.2.2 Suspend/resume The details of suspend and resume are explained in these sections. NXP Semiconductors Universal Serial Bus Controller (USB) i.MX 93 Applications Processor Reference Manual, Rev. 5, 05/2024 Reference Manual General Business Information 2818 / 5652  41.3.2.3.2.2.1 Suspend Suspend Description In order to conserve power, USB devices automatically enter the suspended state when the device has observed no bus traffic for a specified period. When suspended, the USB device maintains any internal status, including its address and configuration. Attached devices must be prepared to suspend at any time they are powered, regardless of if they have been assigned a non-default address, are configured, or neither. Bus activity may cease due to the host entering a suspend mode of its own. In addition, a USB device shall also enter the suspended state when the hub port it is attached to is disabled. A USB device exits suspend mode when there is bus activity. A USB device may also request the host to exit suspend mode or selective suspend by using electrical signaling to indicate remote wake-up. The ability of a device to signal remote wake-up is optional.

[4] [...] Disabling the interrupt masks the request instantaneously as this is clocked by the Arm platform clock. The software should wait for at least three 32 kHz clock cycles before re-enabling this interrupt to allow sufficient time for the request flag to clear.

Disabling the interrupt masks the request instantaneously as this is clocked by the Arm platform clock. The software should wait for at least three 32 kHz clock cycles before re-enabling this interrupt to allow sufficient time for the request flag to clear. Because this interrupt is only used during low power modes of the USB, it is sufficient to enable the wake-up interrupt just prior to entering the USB suspend mode. 64.3.3.3 Interrupts - host operational model For detailed information about interrupt capability that the EHCI host controller hardware provides, see the "Interrupts" section in Enhanced Host Controller Interface (EHCI) Specification for Universal Serial Bus, revision 1.0. 64.3.3.4 Servicing interrupts The interrupt service routine must consider that there are high-frequency, low-frequency operations, and error operations and order accordingly. 64.3.3.4.1 High-frequency interrupts High frequency interrupts in particular should be handled in the order below. The most important of these is listed first because the DCD must acknowledge a setup buffer in the timeliest manner possible. The table below describes the High frequency interrupt events. Table 508. High Frequency Interrupt Events Execution Order Interrupt Action 1a USB Interrupt - USB.ENDPTSETUPSTATUS Copy contents of setup buffer and acknowledge setup packet (as indicated in Figure 352 shows the End Point Queue Head). Process setup packet according to USB 2.0 Chapter 9 or application specific protocol. 1b USB Interrupt1 - USB.ENDPTCOMPLETE Handle completion of dTD as indicated in Figure 352 shows the End Point Queue Head. 2 SOF Interrupt Action as deemed necessary by application. This interrupt may not have a use in all applications. 1. It is likely that multiple interrupts to stack up on any call to the Interrupt Service Routine AND during the Interrupt Service Routine. 64.3.3.4.2 Low-frequency interrupts The low frequency interrupts can be handled in any order because they do not occur often in comparison to the high- frequency interrupts. The table below shows the Low frequency interrupt events. NXP Semiconductors Universal Serial Bus High-Speed Controller (USBHS) MCX N Reference Manual, Rev. 7, 2025-10-10 Reference Manual 2342 / 3763  Table 509. Low Frequency Interrupt Events Interrupt Action Port Change Change software state information. Sleep Enable (Suspend) Change software state information. Low power handling as necessary. Reset Received Change software state information. Abort pending transfers. 64.3.3.4.3 Error interrupts Error interrupts will be least frequent and should be placed last in the interrupt service routine. The following table shows the error interrupt events. Table 510. Error Interrupt Events Interrupt Action USB Error Interrupt This error is redundant because it combines USB Interrupt and an error status in the dTD. The DCD will more aptly handle packet-level errors by checking dTD status field upon receipt of USB Interrupt (w/ USB.ENDPTCOMPLETE). System Error Unrecoverable error. Immediate Reset of core; free transfers buffers in progress and restart the DCD. 64.3.4 Clocks The following table describes the clock sources for USB. See the clock control chapter for clock setting, configuration and gating information. Table 511.

The i.MX 93 includes powerful dual Arm® Cor- tex®-A55 processors with speeds up to 1.7 GHz inte- grated with a NPU that accelerates machine learning inference. The DRAM controller and PHY have multiple external power supplies: VDD_SOC supplies SoC synthesized DRAM controller digital logic, VDD_ANA_0P8 for PLL and PHY digital logic, VDD_ANAx_1P8 for DRAM PLL and PHY analog circuitry, VDD2_DDR for 1.1 V DRAM PHY I/O supply, and VDDQ_DDR for DRAM PHY I/O supply. The SoC may be powered from discrete parts rather than a PMIC, but a discrete-based solution is not necessarily BOM cost-optimized. NVCC_BBSM_1P8 must be powered first and stay until the last. The digital logic inside chip will be supplied with VDD_SOC, which can be nominal or overdrive voltage or a “low drive” voltage. The DRAM controller and PHY have multiple external power supplies: VDD_SOC supplies SoC synthesized DRAM controller digital logic, VDD_ANA_0P8 for PLL and PHY digital logic, VDD_ANAx_1P8 for DRAM PLL and PHY analog circuitry, VDD2_DDR for 1.1 V DRAM PHY I/O supply, and VDDQ_DDR for DRAM PHY I/O supply. For all the integrated analog modules, their 1.8 V analog power will be supplied externally through power pads. These supplies are separated with other power pads on the package to keep them clean, but they can be directly shared with other power rails on the board to reduce the number of power supplies from the PMIC. For the integrated LVDS PHY, MIPI PHY, and USB PHYs, their 3.3 V (where supported), 1.8 V, and digital power will be supplied externally through power pads. The powers to those PHYs are separated with other power pads on the package to keep them clean, but they can be directly shared with other power rails on the board to reduce the number of power supplies from the PMIC. For BBSM/RTC, the 1.8 V I/O pre-driver supply and 1.8 V I/O pad supply will also be supplied externally. The BBSM_LP core digital domain logic is supplied by an internal LDO. [1] FACT SHEET i.MX 93 APPLICATIONS PROCESSOR FAMILY i.MX 93 applications processors deliver efficient machine learning (ML) acceleration, energy flex architecture and state-of-the-art security to support energy-efficient edge computing. i.MX 93 processors offer fast and efficient ML inferencing along with a rich set of peripherals and high-performance application cores for automotive, industrial and consumer IoT market segments. TARGET APPLICATIONS • Automotive: domain controller compute off-load engine, driver monitoring system, audio, speech recognition, cost-effective gateway • Industrial Automation: gateways, remote I/O controllers, industrial scanners, HMI, machine vision • Building Control and Energy: energy meters, EV charging • Smart Home: home security hub, smart doorbell, smart lock, smart thermostat, AV receivers • Smart City: smart lighting, safety and security, traffic control PERFORMANCE COMPUTE ENGINE The i.MX 93 applications processors are the first in the i.MX portfolio to integrate the scalable Arm® Cortex®-A55 core, bringing best-in-class performance and energy efficiency to Linux-based edge applications. Based on Arm’s DynamIQ technology, the A55 core features the latest Armv8-A architecture extensions with dedicated instructions to accelerate machine learning (ML). NEURAL PROCESSING UNIT (NPU) The i.MX 93 family marks the industry’s first implementation of the Arm® Ethos™-U65 microNPU. A dedicated neural processing unit (NPU), Ethos-U65 delivers a combination of performance and efficiency with an optimized footprint that enables developers to create high-performance, cost- effective and energy-efficient ML applications. BUILT-IN MCU A 250 MHz Arm® Cortex®-M33 processor performs time- critical real-time compute and control. It can eliminate the need for an external microcontroller in the system design. The integrated Cortex-M33 core associated with the CAN FD interfaces provides a robust local control network for industrial applications. Additionally, the built-in Arm Cortex M33 in conjunction with the NPU can be used for low-power wake-word detection. i.MX 93 APPLICATIONS PROCESSOR FAMILY  [url] 2 CAMERA INTERFACES AND IMAGE PROCESSING The i.MX 93 family contains MIPI-CSI and parallel image sensor interfaces along with the NPU to support both monochrome and RGB (color) vision applications. The application processor offers a 2-lane MIPI-CSI camera interface capable of supporting 1080-p60 resolution and enables direct connection to external camera module and ISP. The application processors offer capabilities including down scaling, color space conversion, de-interlacing, alpha insertion, cropping and rotation of images for machine vision and other ML-related applications. DISPLAY AND MULTIMEDIA The i.MX 93 applications processors contain a 4-lane MIPI-DSI capable of supporting 1080p60 resolution, a 4-lane LVDS and parallel display interfaces capable of 720p60 resolution. Additionally, it features a high-efficiency pixel pipeline to perform 2D graphics processing to realize cost-effective GUI solutions. It is capable of image rotation (90°, 180°, 270°), image resize, color space conversion, multiple pixel format support (RGB, YUV444, YUV422, YUV420, YUV400) and standard 2D-DMA operations. SYSTEM SECURITY The i.MX 93 family implements security via NXP’s EdgeLock® secure enclave, a preconfigured, self-managed and autonomous security subsystem.

[4] The i.MX 93 Applications Processor is a new CPU generation with many advantages High flexibility based on the latest technologies WHITEPAPER  WHITEPAPER | The i.MX 93 Applications Processor is a new CPU generation with many advantages 2 How does the i.MX 93 processor fit into the i.MX 9 series? 3 Module Designs i.MX 93 processor 5 Mainboard Design 7 Available modules/mainboards of the i.MX 93 processor from TQ 15 Additional Information 18 Content  WHITEPAPER | The i.MX 93 Applications Processor is a new CPU generation with many advantages 3 The i.MX 93 processor How does the i.MX 93 processor fit into the i.MX 9 series? The i.MX 93 processor uses the Cortex A55 core with clock speeds up to 1.7 GHz. The Cortex-A55 processor core uses DynamIQ technology (the successor to Arm‘s big.LITTLE concept) and features the latest enhancements to the ARMv8.2-A architecture with a dedicated instruc­ tion set to accelerate machine learning (ML) models. According to NXP, the i.MX 93 processor is the first in the industry to implement ARM‘s Ethos-U65 microNPU with a performance of 256 MACs/cycle. The Ethos-U65 offers a very good combination of performance and efficiency in a very small size, enabling developers to realize high- performance, low-cost and energy-efficient ML applications. The i.MX 93 processor also contains a 250 MHz Cortex-M33 processor core for time-critical real-time computation and control and the EdgeLock Secure Enclave for providing the security functions. The memory interface is 16-bit wide and supports LPDDR4 and LPDDR4X with internal ECC support. In addition to up to 7 x I²S audio interfaces and 8-channel PDM microphone inputs, the processor offers extensive interfaces: CAN-FD, UARTs, SPI, QSPI, I²C and SDIO. Extensive security functions are also implemented. With the i.MX 93 processor, NXP offers a price- and feature-optimized CPU from the i.MX 9 series. Next to the i.MX 91 processor, the i.MX 93 processor is the smallest CPU in the i.MX 9 series and a good alternative to the i.MX 28 processor, i.MX 6UL/i.MX 6ULL processor for new designs. The main difference between this CPU and its pre­ decessors in terms of graphics and video interfaces is the addition of 24-bit RGB, MIPI-DSI and LVDS interfaces. A total of four CPU variants are available, from single-core to dual-core with/without NPU and qualified to operate at different temperature range The most important interfaces are available as follows: • 1x MIPI DSI 4 Lanes (display serial interface) • 1x LVDS 4 Lanes • 1x MIPI CSI 2 Lanes (camera sensor interface) • 3x SDIO supporting SD/eMMC/Wi-Fi • 2x USB 2.0 • 2x Gigabit Ethernet (1x TSN) • 2x CAN-FD • 8x UART, 8x I²C, 8x SPI, 7x I²S • 1x QSPI • 1x 4-ch, 12-bit ADC A serial camera interface (MIPI-CSI) allows a camera to be connected directly to the CPU and supports its use in digital imaging applications. The i.MX 93 processor is based on the same Arm Core architecture as the entire i.MX 9 series.

rows.context:
[1] FACT SHEET i.MX 93 APPLICATIONS PROCESSOR FAMILY i.MX 93 applications processors deliver efficient machine learning (ML) acceleration, energy flex architecture and state-of-the-art security to support energy-efficient edge computing. i.MX 93 processors offer fast and efficient ML inferencing along with a rich set of peripherals and high-performance application cores for automotive, industrial and consumer IoT market segments. TARGET APPLICATIONS • Automotive: domain controller compute off-load engine, driver monitoring system, audio, speech recognition, cost-effective gateway • Industrial Automation: gateways, remote I/O controllers, industrial scanners, HMI, machine vision • Building Control and Energy: energy meters, EV charging • Smart Home: home security hub, smart doorbell, smart lock, smart thermostat, AV receivers • Smart City: smart lighting, safety and security, traffic control PERFORMANCE COMPUTE ENGINE The i.MX 93 applications processors are the first in the i.MX portfolio to integrate the scalable Arm® Cortex®-A55 core, bringing best-in-class performance and energy efficiency to Linux-based edge applications. Based on Arm’s DynamIQ technology, the A55 core features the latest Armv8-A architecture extensions with dedicated instructions to accelerate machine learning (ML). NEURAL PROCESSING UNIT (NPU) The i.MX 93 family marks the industry’s first implementation of the Arm® Ethos™-U65 microNPU. A dedicated neural processing unit (NPU), Ethos-U65 delivers a combination of performance and efficiency with an optimized footprint that enables developers to create high-performance, cost- effective and energy-efficient ML applications. BUILT-IN MCU A 250 MHz Arm® Cortex®-M33 processor performs time- critical real-time compute and control. It can eliminate the need for an external microcontroller in the system design. The integrated Cortex-M33 core associated with the CAN FD interfaces provides a robust local control network for industrial applications. Additionally, the built-in Arm Cortex M33 in conjunction with the NPU can be used for low-power wake-word detection. i.MX 93 APPLICATIONS PROCESSOR FAMILY  [url] 2 CAMERA INTERFACES AND IMAGE PROCESSING The i.MX 93 family contains MIPI-CSI and parallel image sensor interfaces along with the NPU to support both monochrome and RGB (color) vision applications. The application processor offers a 2-lane MIPI-CSI camera interface capable of supporting 1080-p60 resolution and enables direct connection to external camera module and ISP. The application processors offer capabilities including down scaling, color space conversion, de-interlacing, alpha insertion, cropping and rotation of images for machine vision and other ML-related applications. DISPLAY AND MULTIMEDIA The i.MX 93 applications processors contain a 4-lane MIPI-DSI capable of supporting 1080p60 resolution, a 4-lane LVDS and parallel display interfaces capable of 720p60 resolution. Additionally, it features a high-efficiency pixel pipeline to perform 2D graphics processing to realize cost-effective GUI solutions. It is capable of image rotation (90°, 180°, 270°), image resize, color space conversion, multiple pixel format support (RGB, YUV444, YUV422, YUV420, YUV400) and standard 2D-DMA operations. SYSTEM SECURITY The i.MX 93 family implements security via NXP’s EdgeLock® secure enclave, a preconfigured, self-managed and autonomous security subsystem.
